sections.content:
Some traditional microeconomic theories.

In the later stages, some additional concepts will appear compared to the DSE, requiring extra review, but the overall difficulty of the knowledge points is moderate.

It's worth noting that Tang Rui will cover some knowledge points he favors. It's difficult to tell from the PPT what knowledge points he likes to test. Some concepts may seem very simple, but sometimes you can only solve the problems by following his methods and steps.

He is meticulous in his teaching, responds promptly, and replies to emails incredibly quickly.

sections.content:
The content is pretty similar to DSE Econ before the midterm, except the utility part. However, after the midterm, the concepts would start getting more difficult and require you to have a deeper understanding on graphs (e.g. monopolistic competition, monopoly) and their calculations.
I guess you can manage it if you have studied DSE Econ and do revision few weeks.

His teaching style is quite clear and good, but he puts too heavy emphasis on the calculations part instead of the graphs explanation.
He also replies email really fast (like after 20 minutes or something)

If you like calculations, you should definitely choose him
sections.grading:
I think it is pretty good but the final is way too hard compared with the midterm
you can check others' reviews for the detailed grading rubrics. I think the 3-bonus points are pretty good.

For the problem sets, you will get full mark as long as you complete all the questions, regardless of your answer (i tried to submit some random answers generated by ai and still gets 6 at last for a single homework) I guess it takes around 30 minutes to complete a single one.

For the midterm, it is extremely easy and almost everyone gets over 20 out of 28

For the finals, every analytical questions require a long calculation, which is so annoying for people who don't like maths

I also heard that he gives really good grade (like many of us did get A-range at last) but i dont know exactly the range

sections.teaching:
Wenwen's lessons are very interactive. She often conducts in-class experiments and gives out prizes, e.g. Oreos, to show us that economics is not only about marking schemes and examinations, but also about the theories and logical explanations behind our decision-making. Btw she hates chitchatting during lessons so do bear in mind.

Don't expect TA to provide exam tips during tutorials. If you think you mastered everything already, then don't waste time attending tutorials. Otherwise, you can see which topic you're weaker in and choose to attend the corresponding tutorial session (you can check the tutorial notes to see what TA is teaching for the next tutorial).

-Final Exam-

For both the midterm and final exam, multiple-choice questions make up a large proportion (70-80%).
For the final exam, remember to study for things from the midterm, as they will be tested in the multiple-choice (quite a few of them). For me, I think for the midterm, the short answer is harder, and for the final exam, the MCQ is harder (mainly because I didn't take time to review midterm stuff).
We have to have an A4 double-sided handwritten cheatsheet for the final exam. But no cheatsheet for the midterm.

I think if you studied Econ or DSE before, you will do well and find it relatively easy (according to my friend who did DSE). For me, I didn't do DSE, and I did Econ in summer school during high school, so I found it kinda hard at the beginning, but I found reading the textbook really helpful, especially for the midterm exam. For the final, I ran out of time to study, so I didn't read the textbook. If I did, I might have done better, haha.

sections.content:
For the chapter information, you may refer to the previous post.

In my opinion, the contents of Wenwen's sessions are quite easy. You just need to understand some graphs, light Mathematical Expressions and very simple calculus in lessons. In the exam, basically only some basic concepts will be appearing. For comparatively difficult questions, you just need to do quantitative analysis carefully, and no need to overthink. So, if you are not confident enough in Mathematics, you may come to this session. Just make sure you know how to do basic arithmetical calculation in exam is ok. If you want to learn Econ extremely Mathematically (like me), you may try to reg another sessions, but I don't know who actually put Mathematics heavily inside the exam, and the mean is very low in their session. In general, I think this session did not do Economics in a very Mathematical way. However, the concepts involved are still indeed insightful.

If you are coming from HKDSE, you will uncover how to derive demand and supply curve, very shallow game theory etc. These knowledges will complete the logic flow missed in DSE.
sections.teaching:
Wenwen has a VERY HEAVY MAINLAND ACCENT. If you are afraid of it, then you should avoid coming to her session. However, I think it is understandable, and her lectures can express the Economic Theory in both theoretical way and examples. Therefore, the course is suitable for those who take MATH 1003.

Also, I joined Pang's TA session. I think his teaching is excellent, always expressing idea clearly and sounding interactively.
sections.grading:
You may refer to the previous post for the weighting. Note that all the quizzes and Homework are credit by submission. You just need to finish them to get a lot of final marks.

There are 2 mid-terms. I think both of them are way too easy especially for the second one, as there are over 50 people out of around 250 people getting 90 marks or above. Them means are around 78 to 80, which indicates every student was getting a very high marks.

For the final examination, the mean is 70.38, the SD is 16.31, and the median is 73. The mean and median are much lower than my expectations.

My score:
MT1: 80.5/100, MT2: 95/100
Final: 86.5/100, Final grade A-.
(All HW submitted)

Quite light. You need to finish Homework of course. As they are credit by submission, you may check it carefully after the deadline. Online canvas quizzes are very easy. Just follow the lessons Powerpoints is enough to do them.

You don't need to do tons of exercises, just be careful in examination in order to secure a good grade.

Workload is okay.

For those who are thinking about whether you should choose him as the lecturer, here are some advice:

If you want to choose Econ/ecof/MAEC as you major, I recommend you to choose him as the lecturer. His teaching is so different from other Professors, his way of teaching economics is highly quantitive, and he tells you how to turn economics as a tool to help you make rational decisions in real life given limited resources. He gives you a good taste of what economics really is about in the University level, which is mathematics. If you don't like the his exam style, most likely you are not born for an Econ major, or maybe you love to study economics in a social science way.

sections.teaching:
Robin has a special teaching style. He will talk about many real-life examples of the economics concept and stories. However, his tone is very flat, making it boring. After the midterm, larger than half of the class skipped his lecture. Many people scroll on their phones and sleep in his class. Therefore, if you like listening to stories and are willing to learn real economics, he is a good choice for this course.
In the last lesson, there is a final exam review, in which he will talk about the answer of a mock paper. It is the most useful lecture, so remember to attend it.

For the TA, Jeremy is very good at teaching. He teaches really well. He is local, so he can answer your questions in Cantonese. Also, he explains concepts in a very clear way. If you want to ask about concepts, please ask him, and you will understand very easily.
The tutorial session is also taught by him; it will repeat chapters taught in lecture. However, there will be questions for your practice and more mathematics and graphs. If you love math, you will love the tutorial.

sections.content:
-Difficulty Level: Easy-

Chapter 1: What is Economics?
- Concept involved: None
- Outline: Brief introduction about the course.
- Difficulty: 0/10 -

Chapter 2: The Economic Problem
- Concept introduced: Production Possibilities Frontier (PPF), Production Efficiency, Allocative Efficiency, Opportunity Cost, Marginal Cost, Principle of decreasing marginal benefit, Absolute Advantage, Comparative Advantage, Gains From Trade, Definition of Economic Growth.

- Outline: Some basic economic concepts similar to what had been taught in DSE Econ. PPF is just a way to visualize the total output.

-Difficulty: 1/10

Chapter 3: Demand and Supply
-Concept introduced: Competitive Market, Relative Price, Demand/ Supply, Quantity Demand/ Supply, Law of Demand/ Supply, Factors that Change Demand/ Supply, Income/ Substitution Effect, Equilibrium.

-Outline: Basic economic concepts similar to what had been taught in DSE Econ. Just make sure you understand the difference between every term. (e.g. change in demand and change in quantity demand.) One of the two most important fundamental knowledge for this course.

-Difficulty: 5/10

Chapter 4: Elasticity
-Concept introduced: Elastic/Inelastic/Unitary/Perfectly Elastic/ Perfectly Inelastic Demand/Supply, Income Elasticity of Demand, Cross Elasticity of Demand

-Outline: Explain elasticity with formula and tricks to find the elasticity from the graph. (i.e. supply slope passes through origin = unitary elastic). Be careful that the course adopts arc elasticity instead of point elasticity used in DSE. One of the two most important fundamental knowledge for this course.

-Difficulty: 7/10

Chapter 5: Efficiency and Equity
-Concept introduced: Consumer/ Producer surplus, Market/ Individual Demand/ Supply, Market Failure, Underproduction, Overproduction, Sources of Market Failure

-Outline: Some basic economic concepts similar to what had been taught in DSE Econ. Elaboration of equilibrium, marginal benefit and cost in market scale.

-Difficulty: 1/10

Chapter 6: Government Actions in Markets /
Chapter 7: Global Markets in Action
-Concept introduced: Price Ceiling, Price Floor, Quota, Taxes and Subsidies on Producer and Consumer, and their effect on the market.

-Outline: Some basic economic concepts similar to what had been taught in DSE Econ. Extra content on the effect on the market, provided with some examples.

-Difficulty: 1/10

- Midterm Exam-

-Difficulty Level: Hard-

Chapter 8: Utility and Demand
-Concept introduced: Consumption Possibilities, Budget Line, Marginal Utility, Principle of Diminishing Marginal Utility, Marginal Utility per Dollar Equalization (Utility-Maximizing Choice).

-Outline: Appetizer to the one of the hardest concepts in this course. Budget line is similar to PPF, but for consumption but not production.

-Difficulty: 2/10

Chapter 9: Possibilities, Preferences, and Choice
-Concept introduced: Budget Equatio, Indifference Curve, Marginal Rate of Substitution

-Outline: One of the hardest chapters for this course. Majorly focus on how to correctly draw an indifference curve for different goods, how budget line shift with changes, and how to show the price effect and substitution effect, so as the relationship (substitute/complement) of the two goods.

-Difficulty: 10/10

Chapter 10: Organizing Production
-Concept introduced: The firm's Constraints, Technological/ Economic Efficiency, Principal-Agent Problem, Perfect Competition, Monopolistic Competition, Oligopoly, Monopoly, Four-Firm Concentration Ratio, Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI)

-Outline: Appetizer for the following hell...
While minimal coverage on the two measures, four-firm concentration ratio and HHI are tested in the exam.

-Difficulty: 1/10

Chapter 11: Output and Costs
-Concept introduced: Profit Maximization, Short Run, Long Run, Sunk Cost, Total Product Curves, Marginal Product, law of diminishing marginal return, Total Cost (TC), Total Fixed Cost(TFC), Total Variable Cost(TVC), Marginal Cost (MC), Factor Leading to Shift in Cost Curve.

-Outline: A tons of curve. A clear mindset is needed to understand how to draw all those curves and explain why the curve is shaped like this. It is the time when graphs and mathematical explanations mess up everything...

-Difficulty: 8/10

- Hell mode activated, good luck. -

Chapter 12: Perfect Competition
-Concept introduced: Temporary Shutdown Point, Breakeven Point.

-Outline: Applying all those curves in a perfect competition market model. Understand the characteristics of a perfect competitive market. Understand what the firms and customers can do in this market, and draw the curve. Understand the effect of change in demand and supply in this market, and how equilibrium/ profit maximization is achieved in this market.

Question for this chapter: How do firms make money in this market?

-Difficulty: 10/10

Chapter 13: Monopoly
-Concept introduced: Marginal return and demand relationship.

-Outline: Same as perfect competition (draw the curve for this market, understand how profit maximization and equilibrium are achieved, etc.). Understand the difference between perfect competition and monopoly market.

Question for this chapter: How do firms make money in this market?

-Difficulty:

Chapter 14: Monopolistic Competition
-Concept introduced: Advertising

-Outline: Same as perfect competition and monopolistic competition. (draw the curve for this market, understand how profit maximization and equilibrium are achieved, etc.). Understand the difference between perfect competition, monopoly and monopolistic competition market.

Question for this chapter: How do firms make money in this market? What cause the difference between all those curve?

-Difficulty: 11/10 (The major problem lands on messing up the three market....)

Chapter 15: Oligopoly
-Concept introduced: Game Theory, Nash Equilibrium, Prisoners Dilemma, The Game of Chicken, Bertrand Competition, Cournot Competition

-Outline: To find the Nash Equilibrium for all this model. For the Bertrand Competition and Cournot Competition, either a good math sense to understand the proof or just memorize the result...

-Difficulty: 10/10

- End of the hell-

Chapter 16: Public Choices, Public Goods, and Healthcare
-Concept introduced: Rival /Non-Rival, Excludable/ Non-Excludable, Private Goods, Common Resources, Club Goods, Public Goods. Marginal (social/ private) (benefit/ cost)

-Outline: Introduction to the four types of goods, using Healthcare as an example of underproduction due to differences in marginal private and social benefit.

-Difficulty: 1/10

Chapter 17: Externalities
-Concept introduced: Taxes, Cap-and-Trade

-Outline: Solutions to externalities and inefficiency.

-Difficulty: 2/10

-Final Exam-
sections.teaching:
Instructor: Robin Kaiji Gong
Robin is a nice professor willing to answer students' questions!
(I sent him a Word document loaded with questions before mid-term... and he patiently answered all of them!)
Robin's teaching... is a bit controversial... but I like his teaching style!

2. Robin will draw and explain some hard concepts on the whiteboard. 3. Robin gives us 3 years of past papers for mid-term and final exams.

TA: Jeremy To
Jeremy is the best TA I have met so far!

His tutorial is extremely useful! His explanation is extremely clear, helping us to consolidate all the concepts that have been taught in class.

sections.workload:
Minimal (Medium if you don't have a clear understanding of those basic economic concepts taught in DSE. High if you are also terrible at math)

Homework:
4 Problem sets, usually with 4 questions, with the last one as an open-ended question.
There's barely any workload if your group decides to ask each one to do one question.
If you aim for a higher grade, you might choose to do all the questions once and double-check with your groupmate, which should not cost you a ton of time, approximately 2 hours bi-weekly (per half a month) is more than sufficient.

Exam:
The only challenging part is to fully understand all the concepts. Hence, make sure you can clearly identify differences between all the terms and understand how everything in the model works. (Memorizing is not recommended, there's a ton of curve and everything changes in a different model/ market.)
Finishing all the past papers and understanding the solution is sufficient for the exam.

sections.teaching:

sections.grading:
Very good, with great transparency.

Grading Policies (may change in different semesters)

- Assignments (2% x 5)
Graded on completion.

- Random Quizzes (5% x 2)
If you show up and submit the quiz, no matter what you write, you will receive at least 3 marks.
If you have some slight mistakes, you will receive 4 marks.
If you get it correct, you will receive 5 marks (full marks).
However, if you unfortunately did not attend the lectures and did not email him before the lesson, you will receive 0 marks for this quiz.

- Midterm Exam (30%)
Full marks: 30
Most of the questions require simple mathematical calculations (which I find much more useful), unlike the DSE, which involves a lot of memorization.
The mean (21.38/30) is unbelievably high because I think it is slightly challenging.

So, if you expect the exam to be similar to the HKDSE, requiring a lot of memorization, please consider registering for other professors' lectures.

- Final Exam (50%)
Full marks: 50
Similar to the midterm exam, but the difficulty of the multiple-choice questions is slightly lower than that of the midterm. The paper is a bit long; I finished it just before the “Pen Down" announcement. However, I think the length is suitable (I guess I just spent a bit more time on the multiple-choice questions). Otherwise, the mean would again be terribly high like the midterms.
Mean: 28.52/50, quite normal.

- Total (100%)
Mean: 68.34/100

Prof. Tang is trying his best to give a full range of A grades to his students.

Luckily, I got an A+.
sections.workload:

Assignments (2% x 5)
Problem Sets 1-5

This course is intended for students who have previously studied DSE Economics. For the first few chapters of the course, you can really relax and chill during classes as the concepts are mostly what you learn in DSE.

Starting from Chapter 9 onwards, the content covered are out of the DSE syllabus. You will learn some basic game theory content when you study Oligopoly, which was the part of the content I enjoyed the most in the course. I would say overall, the course content is not difficult at all.
sections.teaching:
Pretty nice teaching, even though she is using the publishers' powerpoint for her lectures, each concepts are elaborated well and she uses different methods to teach / convince us of the content covered. These methods include graph drawing, mathematical derivation and in-class experiments (btw, if you volunteer in one of these experiments, you can get an extra credit on top of what you got in final).

2 lectures + 1 tutorial every week. I personally only attend lectures. But the TA's notes is helpful when preparing for exams. So it would be a good idea to view your tutorial notes even if you don't attend the tutorials.

Even though attendance of lectures/tutorials are not counted towards the final grade, the contents or exercises covered in the lectures/tutorials are typically covered in the exams somehow. Therefore highly recommended going to the lectures, or at least view the lecture videos if you miss the lecture.
sections.grading:
Unlike some professors who likes to add quite a lot of quantitative elements into the exams, Wenwen's exams focus on your understanding of the content, and how well you memorise your concepts. The exams questions are very straightforward, thus you can expect a relatively high mean (82.22 in MT1, 76.41 in MT2, 73.35 in Final). Marking is quite lenient too.

As I said, you can earn extra credits to be added on top of what you earn in final exam. The maximum is 2 points, but Wenwen hosted a Kahoot game in the last lecture, which the winner team can get one extra credit regardless whether you have earned 2 points. So some might actually get 3 points. There will be plenty of chances to earn these extra credits in her lectures, and that might give you another reason to go to her lectures.

A very good professor because he gave us past papers to help us familiar with the question types in the exam.

The TA is also good. You can communicate with him in Cantonese. The tutorial is not compulsory to attend. The content is much more difficult than the lecture but it will not be tested.
sections.grading:
In-class Quizzes-5%
Problem Sets-20%
Midterm Exam-30%
Final Exam-45%

In-class Quizzes:
The quizzes are used to check attendance. But it is very easy, just 1 MC. You just have to answer the question, even though your answer is wrong, he will still give you marks for the quizzes.
There are 6 quizzes, and only 5 of them will be counted. He will not tell you that he will have a quiz next lesson so you have to attend almost every lecture to ensure that you will not miss the quizzes.
In-class Quizzes: 5/5

Problem Sets:
There is a total of 5 problem sets. Each of them counts for 3% and 5% is for Peer Evaluation. The questions are based on the content of the lecture. Just refer to his PowerPoint, and you will know how to do most of the questions.
Problem Set 1: Above mean
Problem Set 2: Equal to median
Problem Set 3: Above median
Problem Set 4: Equal to upper quartile
Problem Set 5: Above median

Midterm Exam:
The mid-term is not very difficult. It is mainly stuff learned in DSE and a little bit of new stuff. Also, he gave us the past paper to help us familiar with the exam mode. Remember to do past papers before exam. Just do revision, and you can have a good result.
Mid-term: Above upper quartile

Final Exam:
It contains more new stuff, so you really have to spend time on revision if you want to get a good grade. Similar to Mid-term, past paper is given to us for revision.
Final Exam: Not released, but I guess not bad

Final Grade: A+
sections.workload:
There is a total of 5 problem sets and each problem set contains around 4 questions. You can form a group of 3-4 people to finish it. Normally, you will have 2 weeks for the assignment. However, some concepts are not taught until the last lesson before the due date. Overall, the workload is not very heavy.
The questions are based on the content of the lecture. Not very difficult to do if you have attended the lecture.

sections.content: Content is not overly difficult. With some overlap in DSE Econ stuff. Could be mastered through practise and understanding. Things after midterm are challenging, however manageable. Would not recommend skipping lessons for Wooyoung lessons. He will include something that is going to be in midterms or finals when he goes off the ppt slides.
sections.teaching: Basically one word. Passionate. He knows his stuff and tries to include some of his specialised econ topics into the course (game theory). Just need to adopt to his mild accent, then u would be fine. Again, do not skip lessons.
sections.grading:
The grading is decent, Wooyoung always emphasises on the grade reflects on the amount of effort you put in. He says he tries to make the difficulties of the paper to a point where the abilities of students can be differentiated. Put some work in the HW questions then you would be very fine.

Got an A range after some hard work. It's quite fair I would say
sections.workload:
Just HW, Midterm and Finals. Both midterms and finals are largely based on Hw. It would be a must to do and understand the hw questions.

Theories mentioned in class should be understood and ready to be applied in midterms and finals. Be aware of minor or subtle changes in questions that would affect the way to answer HW/Midterm/Finals questions.

HW are a bit long, but he gives ample time to finish it. If the whole class has difficulties in completing it, he will postpone the deadline.

If you can do all his extra practice problems (not problem sets), then you are set.

sections.content:
First few chapters are basically slightly more complicated dse microeconomics with some use of f4 linear algebra (marginal cost/revenue etc. ). You can easily grasp the concepts if you have taken Econ before.
The last few chapters (market structure/ international trade ) is a lot more difficult though.
sections.teaching:
basically reading through ppt with some explanations, combined with some iprs question for engagement.She is also very patient and is willing to answer your questions.

Sadly, her voice and the teaching style makes the course quite lethargic.

sections.content: Just some DSE stuff, with some new topics which I think is still easy to follow. If you think it is easy while studying ECON during DSE, I believe this course is easy for you too.
sections.teaching: I attend all lessons before mid term and just some of the lesson after mid term as no attendance is required. I have to say that he is the best teaching professor comparing to others courses' professor which I have taken. He teaches very clear and always uses examples to explain the content. You can really learn things by attending his lessons. Although no attendance is required, still recommend to attend!!! (p.s. I don't attend lesson after mid term is just because it's 9a.m. lesson and I can't wake up lollll. His teaching is good.)
sections.grading:
Problem sets: 10%, 10/10
Midterm: 30%, 26.5/30
Random In-class Quiz: 10%, 10/10
Final: 50%, 84/100

I got a A. I think it is quite good grade as I didn't perform that well in my final exam. (For reference I got a 5 in DSE ECON)
For problem sets and quizzes, you can get full mark by simply finishing them. Remember to attend lessons before mid term and final as the quiz is always at that time.
sections.workload:
Very low workload. Just 5 problem sets (including mc and short questions), and you can form a group to finish it. So I guess everyone can finish every problem set about a hour.
Practice problems before mdi term and final is provided, and it is optional. Don't be scared by the question on it, the exams are much more easier than the practice problems.

sections.content:
Frist part is DSE econ. The second part concerns different market structures and some quantitative methods taught. (calculus is needed!)
Overall, the content is not difficult but she likes to test on some really detail things, so reads through and marks down all the things in PowerPoint. You have to be very familiar with every slide of the ppt for a good grade. (e.g. what is the invisible hand, Is making our decision based on our interest regarded as selfish) Don't worry as 95% of the things in the exam are shown in the slides..
sections.teaching:
It's a clear ppt, but some of the points may be difficult to understand. TA is very willing to answer your questions and reply very quickly even by email. There will be one revision session before the exam by TA, really important.

The YouTube video is also helpful cuz sometimes I don't understand the concept and need some time to digest it.

Both mid-term and final are above the mean by 1.5sd.
mid term: 84/100
final: 86.5/100

cheat sheet is allowed for both mid-term and final
The professor gave out a 25% A range, and my overall score is 89%, getting an A. You need to score 93% to secure an A+.

You can get a bonus by doing a presentation, not necessary but a lot of ppl will do it. I recommend you to do as most ppl just read from their script and make simple PPTs.
sections.workload:
7 assignments but only the best 5 are counted.
80% = full mark
easy to score full marks for assignments

Not much workload if you don't do a presentation.

sections.content:
The content is mostly about economic graphs. It is about consumer behaviors how different market types maximize their profit and how to regulate each and every one of them.
It consists of a lot of graphs as well as a lot of different theories which you will have to memorize.
sections.teaching:
The professor is very active and tries to help us solve our problems regarding the course. She often uses different real-life examples to allow us to understand the topic better.
However, there are some times when her lectures get a bit boring and some of my friends opt to skip the lecture.
sections.grading: The professor places a lot of emphasis on homework assignments and attendance. A whopping 25% of the course grade is dependent on homework and you will only need 80% on each homework to get the full credit. 2 marks will be given if you attend most of the lectures she gives and 0.5 marks will be given for attending most of the tutorials. The mid-term and finals are worth 25 and 50% respectively. These are a bit tough. The mean of the mid-term and final are fairly low so it should be easy to get a B or above.
sections.workload: The workload is very light for a 3-credit course. The workload mostly consists of homework assignments and one voluntary project worth around 3 marks. The assignments are fairly easy and are mostly MCQs or short questions. Based on my own personal experience, the homework assignments can be completed in 75 minutes and you will only need to do 7 of them in the entire semester (and only the best 5 count towards your grade).

sections.content: Just basic DSE stuff before mid-term like elasticity, demand, and supply, and how government policy will affect them, like price floor, etc. But the content after mid-term starts to get hard as they were not taught before like shutdown point and formula for marginal revenue, you might need to spend more time on this course after mid-term if u want to get a satisfying grade. As for the detailed content, you could just read others' comments as they are basically the same every semester.
sections.teaching: Prof Tang is nice and willing to answer students' questions. However, the examples he used to illustrate some economic concepts just made things even harder to understand. But overall, he is good and strongly recommends enrolling for his course.
sections.grading:
midterm 30%
final 50%
In-class random pop-up quiz 2 times, 5% each (grade based on submission, as long as you hand it in, you get the 5%)
5 problem sets (total 10%, also grade based on submission)

For your reference, I did all pop-up quizzes and problem sets. In the mid-term, I got 22/30, regarding the statistics you could just read other students' posts as I can barely remember them. While final I got 97/100.

overall percentage is 90% and I got an A. Even though I got the highest in the final, I performed badly in the mid-term so an A should be fine for me. Friendly reminder for anyone who seeks to achieve A range, try to do all the practice problems before mid-term and final, as they are super useful and can help you to clarify some concepts that you thought u knew well but u don't. It might look extremely hard the first time you do them, but that's normal cuz they are designed to be like this. Just read the answer and try to understand the concept behind them when you don't know how to do it.
sections.workload: 0 workload at all as all the assignments and pop-up quizzes are graded based on submission, even if you did them wrong it is fine. For those who want to ditch classes (like me) but don't want to miss any pop-up quizzes, Tang usually will have the quizzes arranged 2-3 lectures before mid-term and final. Try not to miss those lectures or you will regret losing 5% total grade. IMO, the tutorial is pretty useless and a waste of time attending them, as the TA is just reading PPT. You could learn more by reading the ppt alone and doing exercises. Despite the fact that TA is bad at teaching, he is nice and friendly. If you don't look at his teaching, he is a 10/10 TA.

sections.content: It’s pretty standard beginning microeconomics, nothing special.
sections.teaching: Wooyoung doesn’t require you to memorise any definitions but focuses on having you fully understand the concepts behind each topic. He is very enthusiastic and engaging as a lecturer. He is very approachable, it is easy to ask him questions after class. Everything he tests in exams are covered in his classes. Even though he isn’t really strict on attendance, make sure you attend all the classes so that you won’t miss out.
sections.grading: His grading is lenient even if exam scores aren’t high.
sections.workload: The questions in his exams are very similar to those in his homework question set, which is very helpful. Homework workload is adequate. All the homework are completed in groups. There is one midterm and one final.

sections.content:
The Midterm covered 11 chapters. The final was cumulative, covering 18 chapters. Some were learned in DSE but not too much. My friends from the other sections (different prof) only need to revise 6 chapters in the midterm. Unfair!

Challenging topics (but he loved most, always appeared at practice/ problem set/ past paper/ exam)
Utility, indifference curve
Oligopoly (game theory/ prisoner's dilemma mixed up with Bertrand competition and cournot competition)
sections.teaching:
I could feel his passion for teaching, but sadly, I got confused after attending his lessons. He always said something which contradicted DSE econ concepts or even from his ppt! For example, fixed cost still exists in the long run. He was willing to answer questions patiently. Yet, I was still confused by his replies. I resort to my friends and the textbook. You should buy the textbook when you reg his course! The explanation of the theories was better although the textbook was so wordy.

Don't expect you to quickly absorb the new knowledge/ concepts from the lecture, particularly for Ch8 Utility and Demand and Ch9 Possibilities, Preferences and Choice. I did not know what he was talking about. He always wasted lots of time drawing graphs apart from reading ppt but ppt all had these diagrams.

Be prepared to self-study all the stuff and ask friends if you have questions. He was willing to help students but me just getting more confused.
sections.grading:
In-class quizzes 5% (counted upon submission)
Problem sets 20% (group assignment)
Midterm exam 30%
Final exam 45%
sections.workload:
5 problem sets, posted every two weeks
Each set usually had four questions with division of labour (group assignment)
Not all can be found in ppt. Need more explanation. I even thought some he did not cover in the lecture.

sections.content:
I didn't study economics in secondary school so I don't know how much common content there is. Difficulty is acceptable.

His problems and solutions are mostly quantitative. Not much verbal explanation questions are in the exams. Nothing much to memorize if you review his lecture materials well enough. I personally rank the difficulty as homework < midterm < quiz < final < lecture. Understanding everything in lecture is sufficient. Not all content in the lectures are covered by the practice problem sets, but some are indeed tested in the finals. Some extra review may still be needed even if all practice questions are done.
sections.teaching:
He is the best lecturer for my semester. His slides included everything mentioned in the lectures, so you can skip the lecture (at a risk of losing 5%) if you know everything already and not worry about missing out extra information. I didn't skip any lectures because I don't pre-study, and sometimes his explanation is quite fast so reviewing is needed after the lectures.

If you ask him anything beyond syllabus like rigorous proofs, he will give it to you right away.

TA doesn't care about you at all. He probably just care about getting his work done. No idea what his paper checking session is for. Got every appeal request rejected with irrelevant reasons and some taunting. You should just find the lecturer directly if you believe you deserve the marks. The lecturer did the paper checking session for finals himself.
sections.grading:
5 Problem sets: 10%
2 In-class quizzes: 10%
Midterm: 30%
Finals: 50%

Me: 10 + 10 + 22.5 + 48.5 = 91 (A+)

Problems sets are by completion. Not even full completion is required for full score.

The 2 in-class quizzes on paper will randomly appear in any lectures. Obviously one is somewhere before midterm and the other is somewhere before finals. It is by completion, any attempts will get full score. This is just an incentive scheme for attendance.

Midterm's full score is 30, so 1 mark is 1 final %.
Finals's full score is 100, so 1 mark is 0.5 final %.
I personally think midterm should have more questions.

Midterm is marked by TA, he just look for final answer and either tick or cross everything. He doesn't care about your steps because he just wants his work done. He marked all the papers in one day. In fact he doesn't know how the partial marks should be distributed.

Not sure who marks the finals but it is more lenient and partial marks are much more carefully given.
sections.workload: Light. You can have teammates, but I prefer working alone. Two to three hours for post-lecture review( and homework) every week. The TA just look for completion in homework.

sections.content: Normal stuff. A bit extension based on the DSE. For example, for the oligopoly model, a game theory will be introduced to explain the “interdependence market decisions” taught in DSE. Super fun.
sections.teaching: Her teaching is good with clear accent, which should be rarely expected for a mainland instructor. Super interactive as she keeps asking questions in class though I did not attend any of them. Haha. But the thing I appreciate the most is she keeps uploading the class video on canvas so I can review it though I am super busy in this semester.
sections.grading:
I need to rate an A+ for her grading. Super lenient.  Even though you just get 80ish in every assignment, you will still receive a full in assignment. The grading system is diverted into two streams, the first one 25% hwk + 25% midterm+50% final. The second one 20% hwk+75 % final. Super convenient for me, who is a final guy.

My result:
HWK 25/25
Midterm 76/100. Mean 64 UQ 76
Final 81.5/100 Mean 58 UQ  71.88
Final result: 88.38/104  Grade A

Though the mean of final is quite low, in fact the paper is not that difficult.
sections.workload:
Light workload. For real, super light.
No attendance will be taken.
Homework questions are easy and in lenient grading.
Final is slightly difficult but not that difficult. Just in moderate level. Drilling some years of past paper is more than enough for you to ace the exam.

The course covers most of the fundamental part of microeconomics, as the course introduction mentioned.
Chapter 1: What is Economics?

Chapter 4: Elasticity
Chapter 5: Efficiency and Equity
Chapter 6: Government Actions in Markets

For DSE graduates, please put a close eye on especially the markets. IB has market analysis whereas DSE does not. They construct the fundamental mechanism of determining the prices. You may expect some confusion risen, however you can trust yourself(and the course instructor professor Tang as well) with hard working, you can get the most out of the course.
sections.teaching:
A nice and smart guy. Accent isn't my concern even in US you hear different accents.  In a nutshell, professor Tang teaches in a style that you would not get bored and fade out of focus. I had sat in other instructors' courses, without naming you can notice the reason I gambled in swapping my first course in UST.

Professor Tang illustrates the concepts straight to point, with the aid of examples. Some times I even thought that the number of examples may be too much.

He provided extra practices before the midterm and final, you would get used of the format and difficulty. Moreover, he would warn you and provide reasonable expectation on the exams.

To be fair, no comments on TA as I just attended one tutorial and skipped the rest. It would not affect your grade.
sections.grading:
Grading:
Midterm: 30%
Final: 50%
PS: 10%
Attendance: 10%

So the attendance would be randomly recorded, by completing two in-class quiz on dates chosen by instructor. Regardless of how your performance of the quiz, you would be rewarded in full. Yet no pay, no gain. You can actually learn from the sources.
I got 90/100 in total with midterm and final scoring around 86%.
Final grade: A
I think it's reasonable which reflects my degree of effort and the distribution of the score in class is normal.
sections.workload:
It's all about 5 problem sets(PS) that are submitted in groups, with a group of 4.

If there are some capable IB group mates with you and explain the in depth concepts and realisation to you, then it's quite a good opportunity to refresh your memory and grasp much better understanding in microeconomics.

5 PS in total 10 points would be awarded as long as you submitted in time.

Midterm and final I would comment it as appropriate difficulty. The course is self-consistent that although most of the students have an economic study background, the instructor explains on point. All you have to do is to review the resources you have, and clarify your misunderstandings.

sections.content:
For the detailed syllabus, refer to the file attached.

Midterm: Ch.1-9
Final: Ch.1-20 (The final from all professors are cumulative)
No cheatsheet is allowed.

The content for the midterm is mostly DSE Econ stuff with some new topics that are easy to handle. The content after midterm is a bit harder as you have to be familiar with the calculations for perfect competition, monopoly, oligopoly, and monopolistic competition.

The exams are very different from what was described by the people in 2022-23 Fall, as he noticed the exam was too easy last year. His exams focus on calculations and concepts, instead of solely memorizing stuff. So make sure you do all his practice problems and understand the way of tackling questions in that topic (also try to memorize his answering flow too). If you want an exam for memorizing stuff, reg Yu Yan.

However, your score all depends on the TA, which is an extremely strict marker, so make sure you write every single step clearly, or else he is gonna deduct marks from you, which in some cases are extremely unreasonable and you will have to find Tang Rui to get back the points.

Oh and rmb to enter simultaneous program, very useful in final
sections.teaching:
I didn't attend all his lessons as no attendance is required. But when I attend his lessons, he actually teaches very well and extremely clear, with a lot of examples to illustrate the concepts. However, I usually just read his ppts and that should be enough. He also replies emails pretty quickly so if you have any questions just ask him after class or through email. Going to his lessons help you understand better tho but im lazy lol.

However, remember to go to lessons near the examination dates (1-2 weeks before exam), as he will do random in-class quiz to take your attendance, if you do the quiz then you get the 5%.

Tutorial is useless, TA is useless (bad attitude too dklm).

final: 50%

Assignments passed 80% are adjusted to be full, so normally you will get the homework part all full. Thus, there are bonus given in the following:
1. Attending 20 lectures: 0.5
2. Attend 6 tutorials and ask/answer 1 question: 0.5
3. Presentation during tutorial or present in the form of video: up to 3
These bonus are directly added to the overall mark. They worth a lot. If you dont have time, just try to get the 3 point bonus through presentation.
Cheatsheet allowed in exams. (1 A4-size paper)

sections.content:
Before midterm: PPF and trade, demand and supply, elasticity, government control
After midterm: utility, cost, perfect competition, monopoly, oligopoly (game theory), public good and common resources, externality

Comparing to other prof, Wooyoung emphasizes more on calculation. For the midterm, 80% of the questions is about calculating CS/PS/elasticity etc. He also talks about calculus e.g. proof of AC minimized when MC=AC, formula of MR=dTR/dQ, etc. Could be a good introduction for econ majors.

He teaches more game theory than other prof, extra content including rollback equilibrium and GC mechanism.
sections.teaching:
Very passionate and good teaching. He doesn't rely much on the slides to teach (which is long af, like 50 pages per chapter), but instead uses his own examples in class for students to understand better. He tries to let every student understand the concepts.

Update: Wooyoung is now head of econ dept, congrats!

I didn't give any example but only used verbal explanations, so I only scored 20/50 for it, ruined my entire midterm.

I think I did quite well in the final but after all the result is unknown.

Final grade: B+

In-class Quizzes: 5%
There are 6 in-class quizzes; only 5 of them will be counted.
We will use online mc to conduct the quizzes. The quiz time will not be announced in advance as it is the way for taking attendance.

The grading is good; my midterm received a normal mark, slightly higher than the median. I thought my grade would suffer because the midterm was extremely difficult, and I didn't have enough time to finish the entire paper. However, in the final exam, the difficulty was much lower than the midterm, possibly because no one received very high marks in the midterm. As a result, my final grade was just 1 mark lower than the highest mark in my class, and I received an A+.
sections.workload: The workload is manageable, but it could be challenging for some topics, especially if you haven't encountered them before. Overall, you won't fall too far behind in the lecture if you study each lecture's notes. You also need to keep up with the lecture pace, as some topics might be related to the previous lecture.

Revision tips:

* Don't care about TA practice questions; they are entirely different from the actual paper.
* If you like Mathematics, stay. If you don't like it, run.

He should be more lenient this time.
He likes to ask a question related to Mathematics rather than Economics concepts.
So there is no need to memorise; understanding the concepts is enough.
I did not revise a lot; following the revision tips should be enough to get an A-range.

sections.teaching:
Good teaching, not the best, but I can see Robin trying his best to make the lecture lively. In most cases, Robin relies on his slides, but it is ok because the powerpoints are well-designed, clearly structured, and detailed, just revising by reading the PPT and doing some past paper will get you an A.

Besides, he is helpful and patient. If you ask him questions after the lecture, he is more than willing to answer them for you with the most detailed explanation. Also, one thing that I appreciate so much is that he replies to emails efficiently,

At last, some may think his accent is weird but I found that his accent is better than most professors.

sections.content: The first few chapter is DSE things, such as PPF, demand and supply and efficiency. It will only spend you little time to pick up. After that, there are some new topic that didn't mention in DSE such as utility and budget line, but it is not too difficult to understand. In the later chapter is about perfect competition, monopoly and oligopoly. These topics have been mentioned in DSE, but in this course, it will go deeper than DSE level and is much difficult than DSE level. Nearly all of them are conceptual knowledge and can not learn by rote. Apart from that, the course need to do some basic calculation, but its only very very easy things, such as linear equation. No need to worry if you are not good at math.

For the problem sets, just submit them on canvas on time (even blank paper is fine) and you will get full marks for problem sets (9% of your final grade)

Quizzes are all 20 MCQ on canvas as others had mentioned, you cannot go back once you move on to the next question and they are pretty easy so the mean is high, so be careful when you do the quiz.

She allows 1 double-sided paper cheat sheet for final, but it was so hard so make sure you studied.

sections.content:
Just some basic stuff from HKDSE and some new things. If you are confident in HKDSE economics, you don't need to worry.

Topics covered:

What is economics?
The economic problem
Demand and supply
Elasticity
Efficiency ad Equity
Government Actions in Markets
Global Markets in Actions
Consumers' behavior
Output and costs
Perfect competition
Monopoly
Oligopoly

Most of the contents require you to understand them instead of reciting them. This may sound good to some people. Moreover, usually at the end of each chapter, there will be a huge part of things that are not included in the exam. So the contents to be tested are less than the actual syllabus.

This is a good course for those who like learning because it solidifies your knowledge of HKDSE economics and allows you to learn something new.   

Warning: There are many graphs in this course so be prepared for that xd
sections.teaching: Ms. Zhang is a good instructor. She provides detailed explanations of the course material as well as some tables for summarizations.  There are also some class interactions and 'Economic experiments', which adds some fun to the classroom.
sections.grading:
The overall grading of this course is not bad. If you understand all the contents covered in lessons and try to do some exercise given by the tutor, you will be fine. There are 5 quizzes, 2 midterms, and 1 final.

My grade:
Quiz 1: 19/20 (Mean: 17)
Quiz 2: 19/20 (Mean:16.1)
Quiz 3: 20/20 (Mean:17.5)
Quiz 4: 20/20 (Mean:16.4)
Quiz 5: 17/20  (Mean:16.1)
Midterm 1: 86/100 (Mean:79.8)
Midterm 2: 97/100 (Mean:89)
Final exam: 91.5/100 (Mean:73.7)

Overall grade: A

Note: You can earn extra credits by answering questions during lessons. However, I did not do any of that.
sections.workload: The workload in this course is not light. Apart from 5 quizzes, 2 midterms, and 1 final exam, there are 3 problem sets as well. Each problem set has many questions. It took me around 2 to 3 hours to finish each of them.  There are also 3 self practices, but they do not need to be submitted, which can be a good way to try some questions.

1. What is economics

9. Possibilities Preferences and Choices

Ch. 7 and 14 are not taught. Ch. 16 and 17 were expected to be covered if there was time but we didn't have enough.

Most of the content is basically covered in the high school Economics already with slight variations. Ch.8, 9, and 15 have the most number of new concepts, and Ch. 12-13 have the most extensions. Since only students who have taken Economics will take ECON2113, it is a pretty simple course. Just be sure to expect little differences in question types, concepts, and other items. There are interesting discussion topics and scenarios.
sections.teaching:
Ms. Ding's lessons are very chill. She can talk about a topic for 10-20 minutes without key points (what locals will call 'blowing water'). It is hard to know where the main point is when she does that. If you decide to not pay attention because you already know Economics, it is also not a good choice because you may miss some useful tips, so there is a dilemma.

There is a tutorial every week for one day that teaches the computational skills but the TA, Ms. Chen Kwan, tends to overcomplicate things and the skills are not useful in practice. She usually overruns as well.
sections.grading:
Pretty disappointed at the large proportion the final exam takes up given the formidable difficulty. Very risky class to take even if you only want a decent grade. You may be fine if you are an elite.
There are 5 online MC quizzes with 20 questions per quiz (actually 6 in total but the first one is not counted towards the final score). Each is 8%. Open-book but there is a very bad system that you must make a choice before proceeding to the next question. You cannot return to the previous question after confirming your answer as well.
There are 7 Problem sets in total and the 6 with the highest scores will be counted towards the final score. You already get full marks if you finish them and submit them on time. They take up 9% of the grand total.
The final exam is NOTHING LIKE the usual questions! Extremely complicated and advanced compared to the exercises and assignments. Even if you do well in usual quizzes, be prepared for incredibly hard computational questions. Here are the statistics:
Average 52.1/120
Median 48.8/120
STDEV 19.8
As you can see, the mean and median are both under 50% of the score. The lowest score is 13/120.
Ms. Ding has a fair policy of calculating our final score by shifting more of the weight to the exam or the quizzes according to the method that gives students the higher score out of the two. Details can be found on page 3 in the attached document.
sections.workload:
Pretty light! There is enough time for the assignments.
Quizzes happen biweekly in tutorials but that's also why the progress is a little slow. Something very disappointing is that our final tutorial and quiz had to take place during the study break, one day before my first final exam.

sections.teaching:
Worst economics professor ever.  Chalk-and-talk professor.  Really poor out-of-focus teaching.  Does not have a good grasp on what students know and don't know, and as a result sometimes talks about stuff nobody understands (for example complicated math), and also spends too much time talking about simple concepts.  

Does not have any grasp at all on what students find hard.  No polling questions to test students understanding.  No in-class self-quizzes or asking students questions, so there is absolutely no class participation from the students side.  

Classes involve reading powerpoints only, but she still manages to make it hard to follow.  She even makes simple concepts very challenging to understand, and so you can imagine how it is when she talks about hard concepts.  For example, she never explained the difference between "quantity demanded" and "demand".  If you haven't taken Econ before, how the hell are you supposed to follow.

I attended lectures until after the midterm and I just couldn't take it anymore.  I think I have good tolerance for bad, boring teaching but this is just too much.  I stopped attending her classes and with the help of my friend attended Fei Ding's classes instead.  Fei Ding's teaching was heaven, and her classes were actually inspiring and it really gets your brain juice excited.  Fuck Xuan Li.

Do the best you can to swap Xuan Li for another professor.  If you can't, find someone who attends Fei Ding's lectures and get the zoom code from them.

sections.content: The content taught mainly revolves around the DSE econ syllabus, so if you get good grades in DSE econ, this course should be easy for you. Although it's similar with the content in DSE, you get to dive deeper into each topics in the scope of microeconomics and there will be a few lectures introducing you to game theory. If you like economics, this course will be a pleasure for you to study.
sections.teaching: Professor Lim is very good at teaching and I like his style of teaching very much. He cracks jokes sometimes which makes the lectures fun and engaging. He is a nice guy and a better professor.
sections.grading: The grading is fairly lenient. You basically get what you study for, except if you are really smart or you are really not into it. The curves are pretty high though because it is a course for people who have studied economics before. I guess you can get into A range pretty easily if you get more than 5 in DSE econ.
sections.workload: The workload is pretty low. I had 4 assignments in total for the semester and each assignment has only like several questions. Revision for midterm and final is easy if you got a good professor to teach you the concept well in lectures. Also, no attendance is taken for the lectures and tutorials.

sections.content:
The course is quite easy in the beginning, especially for DSE students. Content for the first few lessons includes basic trade theory (DSE macro stuff), demand and supply, basic concepts etc.. Things get a bit tougher after that, chapters such as utility and indifference curve are completely new to DSE students. Also, note that this course involves a lot of basic calculation when solving problems in assignments and tests (e.g. calculate equilibrium price and quantity with equations of the demand and supply curve), so the question types are quite different from DSE. I do think that it is useful for students that are going to choose econ related majors and provide sufficient basic insight to the microeconomics field.
Lecture content are as follows:
Chapter 1: What is Economics?
Chapter 2: The Economic Problem
Part 2: How Markets Work
Chapter 3: Demand and Supply (1); Demand and Supply (2)
Chapter 4: Elasticity (1)
Chapter 4: Elasticity (2)
Chapter 5: Efficiency and Equity
Chapter 6: Government Actions in Markets
Chapter 7: Global Markets in Action (1)
Chapter 7: Global Markets in Action (2)
Part 3: Households’ Choices
Chapter 8: Utility and Demand
Midterm Exam covers Chapter 1 through 8
Part 4: Firms and Markets
Chapter 9: Possibilities, Preferences, and Choice
Chapter 11: Output and Costs (1)
Chapter 11: Output and Costs (2)
Chapter 12: Perfect Competition
Chapter 13: Monopoly
Chapter 14: Monopolistic Competition
Chapter 15: Oligopoly
Part 5: Market Failure and Government
Chapter 17: Externalities
Part 6: Factor Markets, Inequality, and Uncertainty
Chapter 18: Markets for Factors of Production
Chapter 19: Economic Inequality
Chapter 20: Uncertainty and Information
Final exam covers all the topics taught.
sections.teaching: The teaching of this professor, to be honest, is satisfactory. For a Mainland professor, he does not show much of an accent and explains concepts quite well, however, I would say that his lessons are a bit boring. I did not attend much of the lectures as I  could self-learn the course material, and more importantly, attendance was not a grading requirement for this course(lol).
sections.grading:
Problem Sets  20%
Mid-term         35%
Final               45%
The mid-term exam is extremely difficult, the mean for MT was something around 30% which is unusual for a basic course like this in my opinion. The final, that was conducted online, was much easier though (weird for an open-book open-Internet exam), questions asked were basic stuff in general.
For me, I got 75% in my mid-term and 92% in my final, overall I got 83.7% and it was good enough to grant me an A grade.
sections.workload: The workload is acceptable. Only 1 problem set is distributed per week and each group of 3-4 people submit 1 copy of the answers before lessons. Mid-term and final requires quite a bit of work if you are to aim for a higher grade.

sections.teaching: Focused on theories of each model and takes time to explain why each theory is important in relation to one another. Incorporates real-life examples from time to time and opens discussions making students think critically about real-life problems; applying what we have learnt to the outside world. You can choose on a macroeconomic topic to present to a class and apply theories you have learnt in class to these examples. Research and preparation of the presentation are required. However, the best part of this presentation is that it is marked based on completion and not on how well it is done. It is definitely better to choose to do this mini-project then to let that 10% of your grade go to the final project.

Therefore, the tutorial is supposed to further decrease the workload you have for this course.

sections.teaching:
She explains things very clearly, is friendly and approachable and is happy to answer any questions in the middle of her lecture. She really does her best to make sure everyone is able to follow what she teaches.
In addition to that, she is also good at keeping the class engaged. She asks us questions and asks us to use iPRS on our phone to answer MCQs in class (not graded), to test our understanding.
I must also point out that it was one of the few classes I didn't fall asleep in.
sections.grading:
The grading was decent enough.
Though I wasn't completely satisfied with the way things were done (exams were online because of protests and I feel like I could have done better otherwise), my final grade was decent, I got a B.
sections.workload: The professor really went out of her way to lighten our workload since we are first-year students. So we didn't have any mid-terms, just 5 online MCQ quizzes which were quite easy, and then a final. She gives us homework questions before the quiz which prepares you for the content of each quiz, which I found really helpful and convenient. The best part is that the homework isn't even graded so you can choose to do it at your own convenience.

sections.teaching:
First of all, Prof. Ding doesn't take attendance. In the first lecture, she already said: "attending my lesson or not is your freedom, but I won't provide any make-up sessions because you are responsible for attending the lessons on time".

To be frank, Prof. Ding's teaching is a bit boring. Basically, she directly reads through the lecture notes, which are the powerpoints of the textbooks with maybe some modification made by her. On the other hand, she opts to ask questions frequently. In her lecture notes, there are some MCQs for clarifying concepts, and she may ask the questions through iPRS.

Prof. Ding cares a lot about "concepts". She always asks us to explain certain concepts in a way that "your grandparents would understand". She tries to use many examples so that students can master the skills, not in a way of memorizing but really understanding it. Sometimes the concepts are very different from the DSE syllabus and you may not be able to digest them within a short time.

There is also a tutorial session once per week. I personally think that our TA Peter is quite good. Prof. Ding would ask Peter to explain some difficult concepts in lectures or teach us some mathematical skills that are useful in the course. Peter would give us a handout at the beginning of the tutorial. It contains some key concepts (with explanation) and some simple exercise. Peter would try to discuss and explain all the questions in the handout if possible. He welcomes students asking him questions, although sometimes we may not be able to really solve the problem.
sections.grading:
In my opinion, Prof. Ding is one of the best professors in terms of grading. First, she mentioned in the first lecture that she would give out as many A's and B's as possible (like 15-20% A's or even more). Besides, she provides 2 grading schemes so that students may still have a chance to get a good grade if they unfortunately missed some quizzes or performed poorly in some quizzes.

Components counting towards final grade:
Problems Sets, Online Quizzes and Final Exam (will be explained in detail below and in "workload" part)

Scheme 1
Problem Sets 9% (1.5%@, counts 6 out of 7)
Canvas Online Quizzes 40% (8%@, 5 in total)
Final Exam 51%

Scheme 2
Problem Sets 9% (1.5%@, counts 6 out of 7)
Canvas Online Quizzes 24% (8%@, best 3 out of 5)
Final Exam 67%

Obviously Prof. Ding provides 2 schemes so that students will not be drastically worse off if they performed poorly in either one of the components.

My results: (My final percentage is nearly the same under the two schemes so I use scheme 1 for more information)

Problem Sets 9% (full marks, in which everyone do get)
Online Canvas Quizzes 33.6%
Quiz 1 (Ch. 3-4)         17/20, mean 16.5
Quiz 2 (Ch. 5-6)         19/20, mean 17.2
Quiz 3 (Ch. 7-8)         18/20, mean 14.4
Quiz 4 (Ch. 10-11)     15/20, mean 16.5
Quiz 5 (Ch. 12-13)     15/20, mean 15.1

Final Exam                 38.6%
                                   (75.77/100, mean 51.5, SD 14.74)
(*this year's situation was different from the past, please refer to the "workload" part)
Total percentage under scheme 1: around 81.2%
Final letter grade: A

The highest mark in the final exam was 88.5%, which was one SD higher than my score. Besides, I didn't perform as well as the others in the quizzes because the highest mark for all the quizzes were full mark. However, I still managed to get an A, which was out of my expectation. I would roughly estimate that Prof. Ding has at least given 20% student an A range, which is very generous.
sections.workload:
The workload is very light, or even 0 in my opinion. Apart from the lectures and the tutorials, all you need to do is a few problem sets, which contains MCQs and short/long questions related to the latest chapters taught. The "exciting" point is that Prof. Ding said she won't check the answers of your submission, i.e. as long as you upload something, marks will be awarded.

The online quizzes are also not as stressful as mid-term exams, because each quiz only contains 20 MCQs, in which you need to finish it within 30 minutes. Each quiz only covers 2 chapters, so you don't need to always keep revising.

*Special Arrangement for Final Exam this year
The final exam was changed to an online format regarding the fact that the school campus was closed and all in-campus lectures were canceled since early November.
The final exam was 130 marks in total, which consists of 20 MCQs (2 marks@each question, 40 in total) and 7 short or long questions (ranging from 8-21 marks each). The exam length was 100 minutes.
Although it was called an "online exam", only the MCQs and first 3 short questions were genuinely online. For the remaining 4 long questions, we needed to write all the answers in a piece of paper, then take a photo of the answer sheet with your student ID card, finally upload the .jpg (only .jpg is accepted) in Canvas.
To be honest, I think that the time allowed was not sufficient in the final exam. For example, we needed to finish an 8-12 mark short question within 5 minutes (including time for uploading the image). I was not able to finish some of the first few questions as a result.

Up until when this review was written, I still haven't received any information about the specific scores of each question that I got in the final exam (except for MCQs). Peter only announced the total score after translating the exam in a 100-marks total.

sections.content:
Not too difficult in general. You will learn some DSE-related content e.g. PPF, demand & supply, elasticity and efficiency first, a little bit more advanced but not hard to catch up at all. Next up you will learn some new content, here are a few examples:
1. 'preference, indifference curves': basically teach you how the demand curve and law of demand are derived from
2. 'output and cost': include A LOT OF graphs such that you can perfectly explain how the supply curve and law of supply are derived from (please spend more time on revision)
3. 'market structures': perfect competition, monopoly and oligopoly, something you have learned in DSE before but more advanced and in-depth
4. 'public good': this topic sounds more difficult as it seems, because Prof Lim has combined it with game theory (his research interest) and it might be a bit difficult to follow in the beginning. Just revise a few more times and you should be able to comprehend
sections.teaching: His English accent is not good, so you might have difficulty in understanding what he's trying to say in the first few classes. You will adapt to it though. He made mistakes in class quite frequently when explaining the materials, but I think he's trying to make the class a bit less boring haha. He is a nice professor who will not show any weariness no matter how stupid your question is. The lecture notes are clear and not redundant. He also encouraged us to work hard and shared some of his history, which are absolutely intriguing.

sections.content:
Microeconomics analyzes the market behaviour of individual actors (consumers, firms, governments, etc.) in order to understand their decision-making processes. The course focusses on key concepts in microeconomics and basic tools to understand the allocation mechanisms of markets.
The syllabus is as follows -
Introduction
Demand and Supply
Consumer Theory
Firms and Markets - Output and Costs, Perfect Competition, Monopoly and Price Discrimination, Oligopoly and basic Game Theory.
Market Failure - Public Choice and Public Goods, Economics of Environment
Uncertainty and Information
Note - The content tested is cumulative.

sections.content:
The contents of the course are very similar to the AS and A2 modules of microeconomics in IAL but some chapters have additional knowledge and compared to IAL some concepts are discussed more in depth. However, some of the same concepts taught in this course and IAL now have graphical applications (for example, the price effect of price change of goods which separates into substitution effect and income effect will be illustrated with indifference curves and budget line) and some same concepts don't require graphs (for example the kinked demand curve is not taught for the oligopoly chapter). It also has more but basic maths used as IAL doesn't really teach econ maths.
Chapters:
0. Introduction
1. Thinking like an economists (sounds weird but basically, you are doing this in IAL econ)
2. Specialisation and trade
3. Demand and Supply
4. Elasticity
5. Efficiency and Equity
6. Government meets Market
8. Utility and demand
9. Possibilities, Preferences and Choices
10. Organizing Production
11. Output and costs
12. Perfect Competition
13. Monopoly
15. Strategic Interaction and Oligopoly
17. Externalities
sections.teaching:
I genuinely believe the professor teaches very well, you may think that because you have learnt most of the content in the module (if you studied the same IAL modules as I did) you don't have to go to lectures but I recommend you do go to the lectures as
1. she skims through a lot of content as she does understand that people enrolled in this course have pretty good economic knowledge but does so according to DSE economics, not IAL economics so you won't be bored listening to stuff you already know
2. most chapters have some additional content that is taught which are the ones she goes through thoroughly and I felt that the graphs were understood when explained
3. she gives a lot of good examples and is willing to discuss with students
4. her lectures are actually really enjoyable as I feel like it had a really good balance between teaching course content, in-class iPRS exercises, discussions and most importantly she speaks close to perfect English without much of an accent
5. her slides on canvas are not the same as the slides used in class, the difference being that there are no answers to questions and some blanks that she wants you to fill in in class. But she does upload the complete version on the canvas for final revision.

NB the tutorials had some revision of content from lecture and sometimes new information or application of knowledge. Should go through as although the things taught in the tutorials do show up in the final.

sections.content:
Required textbook: M. Parkin: “Microeconomics,” 12th ed., Pearson International, 2016.

Chapters covered: Chapters 1-7, 9, 11-13, 15-17.

Topics:
- What is economics
- Demand and supply
- Elasticity
- Efficiency and equity
- Government intervention/trade restriction
- Possibilities, preferences, choices
- Costs and output
- Perfect competition, monopoly, oligopoly
- Basic game theory
- Externalities

As the first course in microeconomics, the course is basically the same as HKDSE content with new ideas on how the demand curve is derived, and oligopoly. Nothing extra special in this course.
sections.teaching:
As a visiting professor, Professor Neary does a so-so job for this class. His time management seems to be an issue. Additionally, at times it has been rather difficult to approach him through emails.

He tends to go off track quite often, but to be quite fair, his ideas are often related to the subject, e.g. the beauty contest game by Keynes, Bertrand model, Tobin's ice-cream test. On the good side, he is very willing to answer questions after class, and answers them clearly.

The TA, Icy does a phenomenal job in the tutorials. Her notes are really clear and insightful, and helps one understand the material well. She responds to email very quickly.
sections.grading:
Grading:

Homework - problem sets (group work): 20%
Mid-term: 35%
Finals: 45%

From my experience, it is not difficult to get a good grade in the course. If one attends the lectures and the tutorials, the mid-terms and finals are relatively easy. For the problem sets, only one or two questions count for the grades, the questions are alright.
sections.workload: The workload are basically the 4 problem sets, which aren't that much. Relative to other courses, ECON2113 has a light workload.

sections.content: Content is quite easy. The full syllabus should be listed in others' comments. Overall, it is merely an extension to the DSE syllabus. But beware that some content tested in the exam is only mentioned in the powerpoint but not in the reference book.
sections.teaching: His teaching is terrible and hard to understand, since he stutters quite a bit. I skipped all the lessons after the first few. For me it is more productive and efficient to skip all of the lessons and revise with the powerpoints and reference book on your own.
sections.grading:
There is only 5-6 questions in the exam and the exam duration is well more than enough. With sufficient preparation, one would expect to finish the exam with more than half an hour left. In fact, in the final exam, at least 30% of students have left the exam hall with more than an hour remaining. This gives you an idea of how adequate the duration is.

In terms of the difficulty, it is not that difficult at all, with sufficient revision and practice with past papers and assignments. For the final exam, its difficulty is similar to the homework given. One of the exam questions is literally identical to the last set of homework, so make sure you pay more attention to those.
In the end I got an A. It could have been better had I knew some content tested is only mentioned in his powerpoint slides before the mid term.
sections.workload: In general, the workload is alright with 4-5 set of homework (7-8 questions each). But the last assignment was simply unreasonable, since he only distributed it to us during the study break, which is one week before the exam period.

Most people either don't go to the lectures or show up and don't listen, but I think you should just mainly focus on his own examples, in which he'll take out a piece of paper and start drawing graphs or proving axioms.

The tutor, however, knows the relationship between different concepts very well, and can tell the main points of 3-4 chapters precisely in just a 50 minute tutorial session.

Homework solutions are discussed in tutorial sessions. However professors don't upload and don't allow us to look at the solution (what a stupid idea) and you need to take pictures quickly by your phone. Make sure you attend tutorials and understand the solution as the questions would appear in exams.

sections.content: The content before mid term is the same as DSE Microeconomics. However, the materials covered after the midterm is much harder and include some calculation. Topics covered after the mid term include but not limited to, budget line, indifference curve, monopoly, oligopoly and game theory etc.
sections.teaching: To be honest, her lecture is a bit boring. She will ask questions in the lecture and engage you to think more about the problem. You can skip all her lecture before midterm as materials were covered in DSE syllabus. However, it is better for you go to the tutorials as TA can help you fully understand the course materials and give you some hint for the final exam.
sections.grading:
Two schemes in total. The only difference between the two schemes is that one counts all 5 quizzes and one only counts 3. Since i missed the last quiz, I used scheme 2.

Problem Set: Full (8%)
Quizzes: 59/60 (24%)
All quizzes are open book and in MC format. They are all basic questions therefore the mean is extremely high. Just remember not to miss any quiz as it is much easier when compared to the final.
Final: 133/180 (68%)
Final was much harder than the quiz. Make sure you understand fully the course materials before the exam. Topics in the long questions are mainly the ones NOT COVERED in HKDSE syllabus. Lastly, never miss any tutorials. Part of the hardest question in the finals was covered in the tutorials.

Final Grade: A-
sections.workload: The workload is light. Only some problem set over the term and all you need to do is submit a blank paper. It will not be marked. For quiz, there are 5 quizzes over the term and workload is bearable. Make sure you understand all the course materials thoroughly before the quiz and you will be fine in final.

sections.content: The content is about advanced DSE microeconomics. The first few weeks are about PPF and demand and supply (elasticity and tax), which would be easy if you study E2 in DSE and are familiar with DSE content. Afterwards, lessons need to be attended to learn advanced firm production. Utility, indifference curve, monopoly, oligopoly and game theory is new to us. It would be interesting if you enjoy economics.
sections.teaching: Her teaching is quite good. The pace is satisfactory, and she would ask us questions quite often in the lesson. Feel free to ask her questions after the lesson as she is nice, patient to answer you questions. Tutorial is complementary to her lectures. HECTOR CHENG my tutor is super great, who prepares his own tutorial notes every tutorial. The quiz and final review is really the key point to the quiz and exam. Personally speaking, his concept explanation is much clearer than FEI DING. Cantonese can be used to ask him question also.

sections.workload:
The workload is light. There are five mc quiz in total, testing 2 chapters each, which are quite easy.
8 problem sets in total, which you can just submit a blank word file to get one mark.

However, the final exam (cumulative) is undoubtedly difficult, consisting 1/3 mc and 2/3 long questions. The mc is much harder than the quiz. The long questions testing all chapters are complicated, so enough revision had to be done.

sections.content: Content is 60% similar to DSE Economics. If you got ≥ level 4 in Economics, you should master the course materials with no big deal and get a B grade at least. Topics like PPF, demand and supply, elasticity, government intervention and externality are not difficult to understand. Later, perplexing stuff like budget line, indifference curve, perfect competition, monopoly, and game theory will be introduced. You need to understand the logic behind thoroughly thereafter because reciting everything won't help anymore.
sections.teaching:
Ding Fei's lecture is as boring as hell. You have to really pay attention to what she is talking about lest you can't resist but fall into sleep. In terms of the lecture materials, I would say they are not well-designed because they are too brief. Even the iPRS problems are far too simple compared to those in quizzes and final exam! To fully understand the concepts taught in lecture, you must carefully read through the textbook and make some notes on that.

My tutor is Jason Cheung, a fresh graduate from HKUST Economics. Attending his tutorial is far more effective than going to lecture. You can either listen to an organised summary of the topic or clarify your confusions by addressing to him face-to-face.
